lessons.title: LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime
lessons.summary: Create dates and times, and never forget that they are immutable.

blocks.text: The `java.time` package has three **local** types. Local means: no time zone, just what a wall calendar or clock shows.

blocks.caption: Prints 2024-01-05, 09:30, 2024-01-05T09:30

blocks.title: Seconds are hidden when zero
blocks.text: `LocalTime.of(9, 30, 0)` prints `09:30`. Seconds show only when non-zero: `LocalTime.of(9, 30, 5)` prints `09:30:05`.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `date(2024, 1, 5)` uses a constructor. Java's date types have **no public constructor**: `new LocalDate(...)` does not compile. Use static factories: `of()`, `parse()`, `now()`.
Months are numbered **1 to 12**. You can also pass the `Month` enum: `LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 1)`.

items: `getMonth()` returns the enum (`FEBRUARY`).
`getMonthValue()` returns the int (`2`).
`getDayOfWeek()` returns a `DayOfWeek` enum (`MONDAY`).

blocks.text: Invalid values **compile** but throw `DateTimeException` at runtime: `LocalDate.of(2024, 13, 1)`, `LocalTime.of(24, 0)`, or February 29 in a non-leap year.
`LocalDate.parse("2024-02-05")` reads the ISO format. It needs two-digit month and day: `"2024-2-5"` throws `DateTimeParseException`.

blocks.title: Compiles is not the same as valid
blocks.text: The compiler only sees `int` arguments. It can't know that 13 is not a month, so the error happens when the line runs.

steps.explanation: Months are 1-based, so `2` is February. `getMonth()` returns the `Month` enum, whose `toString()` is the constant name `FEBRUARY`. You'd need `getMonthValue()` to get `2`.

steps.code:
LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2023, 2, 29);
System.out.println(d);
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: 2023 is not a leap year, so February 29 doesn't exist. The code compiles (the arguments are just ints), but `LocalDate.of` throws a `DateTimeException`. Java never silently rolls an invalid date over to March.

blocks.text: Every java.time object is **immutable**. Methods like `plusDays()`, `minusMonths()` and `withYear()` return a **new** object. The original never changes.
`withXxx()` replaces one field: `d.withDayOfMonth(15)`, `d.withYear(2020)`. Calls can be chained because each returns a new object.

blocks.title: The ignored result
blocks.text: A line like `d.plusDays(1);` on its own does nothing useful. On the exam, look for calls whose result isn't assigned. They are there to trick you.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Same idea as Python's `date.replace()`: it returns a new date. The difference is that Java's `plusDays` *sounds* like it changes the object, so it's easy to forget to assign it.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Line 2 and line 4 throw their results away. Only `d = d.minusMonths(1)` sticks. March 31 minus one month would be February 31, which doesn't exist, so java.time **clamps** to the last valid day: 2024-02-29 (2024 is a leap year). No exception.

items: `a.isBefore(b)`, `a.isAfter(b)`, `a.isEqual(b)` compare dates on the timeline.
`isLeapYear()` and `Year.isLeap(y)` check leap years.
`plusMonths` and `plusYears` clamp the day to the end of the month: `2024-01-31` plus one month is `2024-02-29`.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Expect month-end questions: Jan 31 + 1 month, Mar 31 - 1 month, Feb 29 + 1 year (gives Feb 28). The result is always the last valid day, never an exception.

steps.code:
System.out.println(
    LocalDate.of(1900, 2, 29));
steps.explanation: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it is **not** a leap year. `LocalDate.of` throws a `DateTimeException` for February 29, 1900.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `2024-05-04 true`.
steps.explanation: `plusDays(3)` moves from May 1 to May 4. May 4 is after May 1, so `b.isAfter(a)` is `true`. There is no `addDays` or `after` method on `LocalDate`.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile and run without throwing an exception? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `new LocalDate(...)` doesn't compile: there's no public constructor. Month 13 and hour 24 compile but throw `DateTimeException`. `"2024-1-31"` isn't ISO format (month needs two digits), so `parse` throws `DateTimeParseException`.

lessons.title: Period vs Duration
lessons.summary: Date-based amounts, time-based amounts, and which types accept which.

blocks.text: Both print in ISO-8601 format. `P` starts every amount. Duration adds `T` (for time) before hours: **PT**.

blocks.caption: P14D, P14M, PT24H, PT1M30S

blocks.title: No weeks, no days in Duration
blocks.text: `Period.ofWeeks(2)` is stored as days: `P14D`. `Period` never normalizes months to years on its own (`P14M`). `Duration.ofDays(1)` prints `PT24H`: Duration only shows hours, minutes and seconds.
`Period.ofYears`, `ofMonths`, `ofDays` and `ofWeeks` are **static** factory methods. Java lets you call a static method through an instance, so this compiles:

blocks.code:
Period p = Period.ofYears(1).ofMonths(2);
System.out.println(p);  // P2M

blocks.text: Each `ofXxx` call ignores the object before it and builds a brand-new Period. Only the **last** call counts.
To combine, use `Period.of(1, 2, 0)` or the instance methods: `Period.ofYears(1).plusMonths(2)` gives `P1Y2M`.

blocks.title: Only the last one survives
blocks.text: Chained `ofXxx` calls on Period (and on Duration) are a classic exam trick. The code compiles and runs, but everything before the last call is lost.

steps.explanation: `ofDays`, `ofWeeks` and `ofMonths` are static. Calling them on an instance compiles, but each call ignores the previous Period. Only `ofMonths(3)` matters: `P3M`.

steps.code:
System.out.println(
    Duration.ofSeconds(3661));
steps.explanation: 3661 seconds = 1 hour + 1 minute + 1 second. Duration's `toString()` breaks it into hours, minutes and seconds after `PT`. Without the `T`, `P1H...` isn't valid ISO-8601.

blocks.text: `plus(TemporalAmount)` accepts either type, so a wrong combination **compiles**. At runtime it throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException` (a subclass of `DateTimeException`).

blocks.title: A date has no hours
blocks.text: `LocalDate.plus(Duration.ofDays(1))` throws, even though one day sounds like a date amount. A Duration is always stored as seconds, and a LocalDate has no seconds field.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `plus` takes any `TemporalAmount`, so it compiles. But a Duration is seconds-based and `LocalDate` doesn't support seconds: `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`. Use `plusDays(1)` or `Period.ofDays(1)` instead.
`LocalDateTime` has both date and time fields, so it accepts a Period (one day) and a Duration (one hour).

items: `Period.between(d1, d2)` gives years, months and days between two `LocalDate`s.
`Duration.between(t1, t2)` gives the exact time between two times (not plain `LocalDate`s: that throws).
`ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(d1, d2)` returns a single `long` count. Works for any unit: `HOURS`, `MONTHS`...

blocks.caption: ChronoUnit lives in java.time.temporal

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.text: `between(a, b)` is negative when `b` is before `a`: `P-1M-15D`.

items: `LocalTime` has no date, so `Duration.between` never wraps past midnight: 23:00 to 02:00 is `PT-21H`.
`Period.between` counts **whole months** first, then the leftover days: Jan 31 + 1 month is Feb 29, plus 1 day.
`normalized()` folds 12 months into a year but **never touches days**: `P1Y3M40D`.

steps.explanation: Period counts whole months first: Jan 31 + 1 month clamps to Feb 29, then 1 more day reaches Mar 1, so `P1M1D`. Counting days: 29 to reach Feb 29, plus 1 = **30**. The two methods measure differently.

steps.prompt: Tap the first line that throws an exception at runtime.
steps.explanation: Lines 3 and 4 match the right amount to the right type. Line 5 adds a Period (days) to a `LocalTime`, which has no day field: `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`. Line 6 would also throw, but it is never reached.

lessons.title: Instant & ZonedDateTime
lessons.summary: Points on the global timeline, zones, offsets and converting between them.

blocks.text: An `Instant` is a point on the timeline, counted from the **epoch**: 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. The `Z` means UTC. It has no zone and no calendar fields.

blocks.code:
System.out.println(Instant.ofEpochSecond(0));
System.out.println(Instant.ofEpochSecond(86400));

items: `Instant.now()` is the current moment.
You can add seconds, minutes, hours and days.
Months and years throw `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`: their length depends on a calendar and zone, which Instant doesn't have.

blocks.text: A `ZoneId` is a region with rules, like `"Europe/Paris"`. A `ZoneOffset` is a fixed shift from UTC, like `+02:00`. A region's offset can change during the year (summer time).

blocks.caption: Offset, then the zone in brackets

blocks.text: An unknown ID such as `ZoneId.of("Mars/Base")` throws `ZoneRulesException`, a subclass of `DateTimeException`.

blocks.title: Converting
blocks.text: `z.toInstant()` gives the UTC moment. `instant.atZone(zone)` and `localDateTime.atZone(zone)` go the other way.

steps.explanation: In June, Paris is at UTC+02:00. Noon in Paris is two hours **earlier** in UTC: 10:00. `toInstant()` always prints UTC with a `Z`.

steps.title: Same instant or same local time?

blocks.text: Changing a ZonedDateTime's zone has two meanings:

items: `withZoneSameInstant(zone)`: same moment, different wall clock. Use it to answer "what time is it in Tokyo now?"
`withZoneSameLocal(zone)`: same wall clock, different moment. The local date and time stay, only the zone changes.

blocks.title: equals vs isEqual
blocks.text: `equals()` compares date, time, offset **and** zone. Two ZonedDateTimes for the same moment in different zones are not `equals`. Use `isEqual()` (or `compareTo`) to compare moments.

steps.explanation: Paris is +02:00 and Tokyo +09:00 in June, so 12:00 in Paris is 19:00 in Tokyo. `withZoneSameInstant` keeps the moment, so `isEqual` is `true`.
Both objects represent the same moment, so `isEqual` is `true`. But `equals` also compares the zone, and UTC is not America/New_York, so `equals` is `false`. The output is `false true`.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `9`.
steps.explanation: `Instant.atZone(zone)` returns a `ZonedDateTime`. The epoch is midnight UTC, which is 09:00 in Tokyo (+09:00), so `getHour()` prints 9. `getOffset()` would print `+09:00`.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Adding one day to an Instant is fine. Adding a month is not: a month's length depends on the calendar, and Instant has none. It throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: An Instant always represents a moment in UTC.
withZoneSameLocal keeps the same moment on the timeline.
ZonedDateTime's toString() shows the offset and the zone ID in brackets.
ZoneId.of with an unknown ID returns null.
steps.explanation: `withZoneSameLocal` keeps the wall-clock time, so the moment changes. `LocalDateTime` has no zone at all. An unknown zone ID throws `ZoneRulesException`; java.time factories don't return null.

lessons.title: Daylight saving time
lessons.summary: Gaps, overlaps and why a day isn't always 24 hours.

blocks.text: A region like `America/New_York` changes its offset for summer time. The exam loves these days because local times behave strangely.

blocks.title: Spring forward, fall back
blocks.text: In spring an hour is **skipped** (a gap). In fall an hour is **repeated** (an overlap). You'll always be given the dates on the exam.
On March 10, 2024 the local times 2:00 to 2:59 never happen in New York. If you create one anyway, `ZonedDateTime` does not throw. It moves the time **forward by the length of the gap** (one hour).

blocks.caption: 2:30 doesn't exist, so you get 3:30 EDT

blocks.title: No exception in the gap
blocks.text: A non-existent local time is adjusted, not rejected. Only truly invalid values (hour 25, February 30) throw.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: 2:15 falls in the spring gap. `ZonedDateTime.of` shifts it forward by one hour to 3:15, and after the jump New York is at -04:00.

blocks.text: On November 3, 2024 the hour from 1:00 to 1:59 happens **twice**: first at -04:00, then again at -05:00.

items: `ZonedDateTime.of` picks the **earlier** offset (-04:00).
`withLaterOffsetAtOverlap()` switches to the second one (-05:00).
Adding one hour to 1:30-04:00 gives 1:30-05:00: same wall clock, one real hour later.

steps.explanation: 1:30 is in the overlap, so `of` picks the earlier offset, -04:00. One real hour later the clocks have fallen back, so the wall clock shows 1:30 again, now at -05:00.

items: `plusDays(1)` keeps the **local time** and adjusts the offset. The real elapsed time can be 23 or 25 hours.
`plusHours(24)` adds exactly 24 real hours. The wall clock may then show a different hour.
`Duration.between` measures real time, so a DST day is `PT23H` or `PT25H`.

blocks.caption: The spring day has only 23 hours

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: When a question crosses a DST date, ask: is it adding a **date** amount (days, Period) or a **time** amount (hours, Duration)? Date amounts keep the clock time; time amounts keep the real elapsed time.

steps.explanation: Clocks jump forward overnight, so 24 real hours after noon on March 9 the clock shows 13:00. `plusDays(1)` keeps 12:00 local, but only 23 real hours pass, so the Duration is `PT23H`.
November 3 has the repeated hour, so from midnight to the next midnight 25 real hours pass: `PT25H`.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `-05:00`.
steps.explanation: 1:30 on November 3 happens twice. `of` picks the earlier offset (-04:00), and `withLaterOffsetAtOverlap()` picks the second occurrence at -05:00. `withFixedOffsetZone()` would keep -04:00.

steps.prompt: In zone America/New_York, which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: ZonedDateTime.of throws an exception for a time in the spring gap.
steps.explanation: Spring creates a gap and fall creates an overlap. `plusDays` keeps local time, so it can add 23 or 25 real hours. A gap time is shifted forward, not rejected. In July New York is on EDT, -04:00.

lessons.title: Formatting & parsing dates
lessons.summary: DateTimeFormatter patterns, ISO formats and the exceptions they throw.

blocks.text: `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(...)` builds a formatter from letters. It lives in `java.time.format`.

blocks.caption: July 4, 2024 at 15:05

blocks.text: You don't always need a pattern. `ofLocalizedDate`, `ofLocalizedTime` and `ofLocalizedDateTime` take a `FormatStyle` (`SHORT`, `MEDIUM`, `LONG`, `FULL`) and format the way a locale expects. `withLocale` picks the locale.

blocks.title: Localized styles need the right fields
blocks.text: A time style on a `LocalDate` throws. `LONG` and `FULL` **time** styles print a zone, so formatting a `LocalDateTime` with `ofLocalizedDateTime(FormatStyle.LONG)` throws `DateTimeException`. An `Instant` has no date fields at all: give the formatter a zone with `withZone(...)`.

blocks.caption: No zone to print

items: `MM` is month, `mm` is minute.
`HH` is 0-23, `hh` is 1-12 (use with `a`).
Text that isn't a pattern goes in **single quotes**: `'at'`. Two single quotes `''` print one quote.
Unknown letters throw `IllegalArgumentException` when `ofPattern` runs.

blocks.title: Unquoted words
blocks.text: `ofPattern("HH:mm at")` doesn't print "at". Every letter is a pattern letter: `a` is AM/PM and `t` is unknown, so `ofPattern` throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `strftime` uses `%` codes (`%Y-%m-%d`). Java has no `%`: plain letters are codes, and literal text must be quoted.

blocks.title: y vs Y
blocks.text: `y` is the calendar year. `Y` is the **week-based** year, which differs in the last days of December and the first days of January. `Q` is the quarter (`Q` 4, `QQQ` Q4). For ISO week numbers use `IsoFields.WEEK_OF_WEEK_BASED_YEAR` or `DateTimeFormatter.ISO_WEEK_DATE`.

blocks.caption: Dec 30, 2024 is in week 1 of 2025

steps.explanation: `hh` is the 12-hour clock, so 15 becomes `03`. `mm` is minutes (`05`), `dd` the day (`04`) and `MM` the month (`07`).

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The pattern is just a String, so it compiles. When `ofPattern` parses it, `a` is AM/PM and `t` is not a pattern letter: `IllegalArgumentException`. Write `'at'` in quotes to print literal text.

blocks.text: A formatter can only print fields the object has. Formatting a `LocalDate` with `HH` or a `LocalTime` with `yyyy` compiles but throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`.
You can format in either direction; both do the same thing:

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: When you see a pattern, check each letter against the type. `mm` on a `LocalDate` is a sneaky one: it asks for minutes, which a date doesn't have.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `LocalDate` has no hour or minute. The formatter asks for `HH`, so `format` throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`. Java never fills in midnight for you.

items: `LocalDate.parse("2024-07-04")` uses ISO format by default.
`LocalDate.parse(text, formatter)` uses your pattern.
Text that doesn't match, or lacks a needed field, throws `DateTimeParseException`.
Built-in ISO formatters: `ISO_LOCAL_DATE` (2024-07-04), `ISO_LOCAL_TIME`, `ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME`.

blocks.title: format vs parse
blocks.text: `format` turns an object into text. `parse` is static on the target type and turns text into an object.
`LocalTime.parse("09:30")` and `LocalDateTime.parse("2024-07-04T09:30")` work the same way: ISO by default, `DateTimeParseException` otherwise.

steps.prompt: Complete the pattern so the code prints `2024-07-04T15:05`.
steps.explanation: The month needs `MM` (`mm` means minutes). Hour 15 needs `HH`: `hh` only accepts 1-12, so parsing 15 would throw `DateTimeParseException`.

steps.prompt: Given `d = LocalDate.of(2024, 7, 4)` and `t = LocalTime.of(9, 5)`, which two lines throw an exception at runtime? `ofPattern` and `ISO_LOCAL_DATE` are statically imported from `DateTimeFormatter`. Choose two.
steps.explanation: `H` asks a LocalDate for an hour: `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`. The default `parse` expects ISO dashes, so slashes give `DateTimeParseException`. The other lines only use fields the type has.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that throws an exception.
steps.explanation: Formatting only prints some fields, so `MM/dd` works for output (`01/02`). Parsing must build a full LocalDate, and the text has no year: `DateTimeParseException`.

lessons.title: Locale
lessons.summary: Languages, regions, the default locale and its categories.

blocks.text: A `java.util.Locale` describes a language and, optionally, a country or region. `toString()` joins them with an underscore: language **lowercase**, country **uppercase**.

items: `Locale.of(language)` and `Locale.of(language, country)` are the factories since Java 19.
`new Locale("en", "US")` still compiles but is **deprecated** (only a warning).
`Locale.forLanguageTag("fr-CA")` reads the IETF tag with a hyphen.
`new Locale.Builder().setLanguage("en").setRegion("US").build()`

blocks.code:
System.out.println(Locale.of("FR", "ca"));
System.out.println(Locale.GERMAN);
blocks.caption: Case is normalized: fr_CA, then de

blocks.title: Locale.ROOT
blocks.text: `Locale.ROOT` has an empty language and country. It matches the **base** resource bundle, and is the safe choice for text that must not change by locale: `s.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)` behaves the same everywhere, while Turkish turns `i` into a dotted capital `İ`.

steps.explanation: `Locale.of` normalizes case: language lowercase, country uppercase. `Locale.GERMAN` is language only (`de`); `Locale.GERMANY` would be `de_DE`. `toString` uses `_`, not `-`.
Builder setters can be called in any order. `build()` produces language `en` and region `US`, printed as `en_US`.

steps.prompt: `new Locale("en", "US")` fails to compile in Java 21.
steps.code:
Locale l = new Locale("en", "US");
System.out.println(l);
steps.explanation: The constructors were deprecated in Java 19, but deprecation only causes a compiler **warning**. The code compiles and prints `en_US`. Prefer `Locale.of("en", "US")` in new code.

blocks.text: `Locale.getDefault()` returns the JVM's default, taken from the OS. `Locale.setDefault(l)` changes it for the whole JVM.
There are two **categories**:

items: `Locale.Category.FORMAT`: numbers, dates, currencies.
`Locale.Category.DISPLAY`: names shown to the user, like a language name.
`setDefault(Locale)` sets the default **and** both categories.
`setDefault(Category, Locale)` changes only that category.
`getDefault()` with no argument is not tied to either category.

blocks.caption: DISPLAY is still en_US

blocks.title: Always pass a Locale
blocks.text: Formatters without a Locale argument use the default, so output changes from machine to machine. Pass one explicitly when the output matters.

steps.explanation: The second call only changes the FORMAT category. `getDefault()` without an argument keeps returning `en_US`; `getDefault(FORMAT)` returns `fr_FR`.

steps.prompt: Which two expressions give a Locale for French as spoken in Canada? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `Locale.CANADA` is English (`en_CA`). Swapping the arguments gives language `ca` and country `FR`. `Locale.of("fr-CA")` treats the whole string as a language (`fr-ca`); use `forLanguageTag` for hyphenated tags.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `es_MX`.
steps.explanation: The nested class is `Locale.Builder` and the setter for the language is `setLanguage`. It pairs with `setRegion` for the country.

lessons.title: Resource bundles
lessons.summary: Look up translated text and know exactly which bundle Java picks.

blocks.text: A **resource bundle** is a set of key/value pairs for one locale. All bundles in a family share a **base name**, followed by the locale:

blocks.code:
Labels.properties        (base, default text)
Labels_fr.properties     (French)
Labels_fr_CA.properties  (French, Canada)
blocks.caption: baseName_language_COUNTRY.properties

blocks.text: A `.properties` file is lines of `key=value`. You load a bundle and read keys:
A bundle can also be a Java class with the same name that extends `ListResourceBundle` and returns its pairs from `getContents()`. If a class and a properties file have the same name, the class wins.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Think of each bundle as a dict, with Java walking a chain of dicts for you. `getString` on a missing key never returns `None` or `null`: it throws `MissingResourceException`.
`getBundle("Labels", fr_CA)` with default locale `en_US` tries these names **in order** and stops at the first one that exists:

items: `Labels_fr_CA` (requested language + country)
`Labels_fr` (requested language)
`Labels_en_US` (default language + country)
`Labels_en` (default language)
`Labels` (base)

blocks.text: If none exists, `getBundle` throws `MissingResourceException`.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: The default locale is only tried when **no** bundle for the requested locale exists. Requesting `de` with default `en_US` goes to `Labels_en` if it exists, before the base `Labels`.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `Labels_fr` matches the requested language, so it's chosen. It has `hi`, but not `bye`, so `bye` comes from its parent, the base `Labels`. `Labels_en` is never consulted.

steps.prompt: Same bundles, default locale `en_US`. What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: There's no `Labels_de_DE` or `Labels_de`, so Java falls back to the default locale and finds `Labels_en`. Its `hi` is `Hi`; `bye` comes from the base `Labels`.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. Put the bundle names in the order `getBundle("Labels", Locale.of("fr", "CA"))` tries them.
steps.explanation: Most specific requested locale first, then the requested language, then the default locale (country, then language), and finally the base bundle. There is never a country-only name like `Labels_CA`.

blocks.text: Once a bundle is chosen, a key is looked up in that bundle and then in its **parents**: `Labels_fr_CA` → `Labels_fr` → `Labels`.
The default-locale bundles are **not** parents. A key that exists only in `Labels_en` is invisible when `Labels_fr` was chosen.

blocks.title: Missing key = exception
blocks.text: If no bundle in the parent chain has the key, `getString` throws `MissingResourceException` at runtime. It never returns null.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `Labels_fr` is chosen. Its parent chain is `Labels_fr` → `Labels`, and neither has `bye`. `Labels_en` has it, but default-locale bundles aren't parents, so `getString` throws `MissingResourceException`.

steps.prompt: Only `Labels` and `Labels_fr` exist and the default locale is `en_US`. `getBundle("Labels", Locale.GERMAN)` returns the base bundle `Labels`.
steps.explanation: Nothing matches German, and nothing matches the default `en_US` or `en`. The base bundle is the last candidate, so it's returned. Only if `Labels` were missing too would `getBundle` throw `MissingResourceException`.

steps.prompt: Which two are valid file names in the resource bundle family with base name `Labels`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Bundle names join base name, language and country with **underscores**: `Labels_de`, `Labels_fr_CA`. Hyphens and dots are never part of the generated candidate names, so those files are never found.

blocks.text: `java.text.NumberFormat` formats numbers for a locale. Pick a factory, then call `format`:

blocks.title: Rounding is half-even
blocks.text: NumberFormat rounds **half-even** by default. 12.5% becomes `12%` (round to the even neighbour), not 13%.

blocks.title: Compact numbers
blocks.text: `getCompactNumberInstance(Locale.US, NumberFormat.Style.SHORT)` gives `1K`, `3K` (for 2,600), `1M`. `Style.LONG` spells it out: `2 million`.
`getInstance(locale)` shows at most **3** fraction digits (rounded half-even) and uses the locale's symbols. In German the grouping separator is `.` and the decimal separator is `,`.

`java.util.Currency` describes a currency: `Currency.getInstance("JPY")` by ISO code, or `Currency.getInstance(locale)` for a country's currency. `getCurrencyInstance(locale)` uses that locale's currency, separators and symbol position, e.g. `1.234,50 €` for Germany.

blocks.caption: Yen has no minor unit

steps.explanation: The US currency format puts `$` first, groups thousands with commas and always shows two decimals.

items: `nf.parse(text)` returns a `Number` (use `intValue()`, `doubleValue()`...).
It reads as far as it can and **ignores trailing text**: `"1,234.5abc"` gives 1234.5.
If the text doesn't **start** with a number, it throws `ParseException`, a **checked** exception.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Because `ParseException` is checked, code calling `parse` must catch it or declare `throws`. Watch for that before reading the logic.

steps.prompt: This code is inside `main(...) throws Exception`. What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `parse` stops at `kg` and returns 2500.75. `intValue()` truncates to 2500, plus 1 is 2501. Trailing text is not an error; only text that doesn't start with a number is.

rows: digit, padded with zero if missing

blocks.title: Locale symbols
blocks.text: `new DecimalFormat(pattern)` uses the default FORMAT locale's symbols. In `en_US`, `,` and `.` print as themselves.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. What is the output?
steps.explanation: `000.0#` forces three integer digits and at least one decimal: `007.5` (the `#` adds nothing because there's no second decimal). `#,###.##` groups thousands and keeps at most two decimals, rounding .678 to .68.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. Complete the pattern so the code prints `0042.10`.
steps.code:
var f = new DecimalFormat("___");
System.out.println(f.format(42.1));
steps.explanation: Every `0` forces a digit, so four zeros before the point pad `42` to `0042` and two after pad `.1` to `.10`. With `#` after the point (`0000.##`) you'd get `0042.1`.

blocks.text: `MessageFormat.format(pattern, args...)` fills numbered placeholders `{0}`, `{1}`... in any order. Numbers are formatted with the default locale: `{0}` with 12345 gives `12,345`.

blocks.code:
System.out.println(MessageFormat.format(
    "{1} owes {0}", "Ann", "Bob"));

blocks.title: Single quotes
blocks.text: In MessageFormat a single quote starts quoted text. `"It's {0}"` prints `Its {0}`. Write `''` for one apostrophe: `"It''s {0}"`.
A placeholder can name a **subformat**: `{0,number,#.##}`, `{0,number,percent}`, `{0,number,integer}`, `{0,date,short}`. Text in single quotes is literal, so `'{0}'` prints the braces.
A wrong type, like `%d` with a String, compiles but throws `IllegalFormatConversionException`.

To **sort** text the way a language expects, use `java.text.Collator.getInstance(locale)`. It implements `Comparator<Object>`, so you can pass it to `sort`. `String`'s natural order compares char codes, so every capital comes before every lowercase letter.

blocks.title: Collator strength
blocks.text: `setStrength(Collator.PRIMARY)` ignores case and accents, so `compare("a", "A")` returns 0. `SECONDARY` also notices accents; `TERTIARY` (the default) also notices case.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. What is the output?
steps.explanation: `{1}` is the second argument, `"Cart"`, and `{0}` the first, 1200. MessageFormat formats numbers with grouping, so 1200 prints as `1,200`.

steps.prompt: The default locale is `en_US`. What is the output?
steps.code:
System.out.println(String.format(
    "%d|%.2f|%,d", 7, 3.14159, 98765));
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `%d` prints 7, `%.2f` rounds to two decimals (3.14) and `%,d` adds grouping commas (98,765).

steps.prompt: This code compiles, but throws an exception at runtime.
steps.code:
System.out.println(
    String.format("%d", "5"));
steps.explanation: The format string is only checked when it runs. `%d` needs an integer type, and `"5"` is a String, so `String.format` throws `IllegalFormatConversionException`.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile and run without throwing an exception? Choose two.
steps.explanation: All five compile because `plus` takes any `TemporalAmount`. A LocalDate can't take hours, a LocalTime can't take days, and an Instant can't take months: each throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`.

The percent format multiplies by 100 and shows no decimals by default: 25.6 rounds to 26.
